facts.clinical_statement: Woman with recurrent left-leg DVT after anticoagulation interruption

evidence.quote: 53-year-old woman
presented with acute-onset left lower extremity swelling and pain at a hospital along her long-haul trucking route.

Deep venous thrombosis (DVT), either as an initial or recurrent event, is a common problem hematologists encounter while caring for hospital inpatients. It is caused by a variety of factors, sometimes anatomic in nature, and is managed with medical anticoagulation and, in some cases, procedural interventions such as mechanical thrombectomy. A 53-year-old woman, with a history of DVT of the lower extremity four years prior, presented to the emergency department with rapid development of swelling and pain in the left lower extremity after missing two doses of her anticoagulant. She was found to have an occlusive DVT in the left lower extremity requiring surgical thrombectomy. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed the absence of the inferior vena cava with collaterals draining into the azygos vein. She had negative thrombophilia testing. The initial and recurrent thrombotic events were attributed to stagnant and turbulent blood flow due to anomalous venous drainage from the lower extremities.

The patient was started on a heparin infusion for anticoagulation and was evaluated by vascular surgery, who took her for percutaneous transluminal venous thrombectomy of the left lower extremity, with operative findings of an acute-on-chronic DVT. A mechanical thrombectomy was performed through a 16 French lightning catheter, followed by balloon angioplasty with a 12 mm x 4 cm high-pressure balloon of a tight stenosis in the left common iliac vein with stenting using a 20 mm x 80 mm wallstent. Post-dilation was performed with a 14 mm x 4 cm high-pressure balloon, and further mechanical thrombectomy was performed, with venography showing patent vessels thereafter. She experienced rapid and dramatic improvement in her symptoms after mechanical thrombectomy and was transitioned from infusional heparin back to rivaroxaban for outpatient anticoagulation. She was discharged on postoperative day 2.

fields.action_text: Authors recommend indefinite anticoagulation for persistent anatomic recurrence risk; actual long-term implementation not documented

facts.clinical_statement: Indefinite anticoagulation indicated in author discussion

evidence.quote: thus indicating indefinite anticoagulation to prevent recurrence

The risk of recurrent DVT in patients with an unprovoked clot after three months of anticoagulation, when anticoagulation is stopped, is about 10% in the first year []. Risk factors for recurrent DVT include male sex, presence of both DVT and PE at the time of the initial event, and persistent provoking risk factors []. We hypothesize that the patient suffered from a rapid recurrence of DVT due to her underlying IVC agenesis as a non-modifiable provoking risk factor, especially in light of the absence of other thrombophilic conditions. Our recommendation for management of these patients is advising indefinite anticoagulation in consideration of a non-modifiable risk factor, as has been suggested by a previous retrospective, observational study, which demonstrated lower recurrent DVT risk in patients with IVC agenesis on indefinite anticoagulation [].

facts.notes: Discussion-level recommendation for persistent anatomic risk; discharge drug actual rivaroxaban. No lifelong adherence/outcome asserted.

evidence.quote: Congenital absence of the IVC is a rare anatomic anomaly that is only seen in about 0.0005% and 1% of the population []. In young patients with otherwise unexplained deep vein thrombosis, it can be present in up to 5% of cases []. One can easily and rationally conceptualize that the absence of this large caliber vessel would cause turbulence and relatively static venous return to the heart, predisposing to thrombotic events as part of a virtual triad as mentioned above. Interestingly, our patient had never experienced DVT symptoms prior to her first event four years prior to this presentation. She had adapted to the absence of the IVC through the development of large collateral venous structures that drained into the azygous vein to reach the central circulation. Azygos continuation of the IVC in the setting of congenital agenesis of the IVC has previously been reported in other cases []. The employment of the present patient as a long-haul truck driver caused further venous stasis on top of that posed by her anatomic anomaly and interruption in anticoagulation, which led to the rapid development of recurrent DVT.

evidence.quote: 53-year-old woman
presented with acute-onset left lower extremity swelling and pain at a hospital along her long-haul trucking route.

Deep venous thrombosis (DVT), either as an initial or recurrent event, is a common problem hematologists encounter while caring for hospital inpatients. It is caused by a variety of factors, sometimes anatomic in nature, and is managed with medical anticoagulation and, in some cases, procedural interventions such as mechanical thrombectomy. A 53-year-old woman, with a history of DVT of the lower extremity four years prior, presented to the emergency department with rapid development of swelling and pain in the left lower extremity after missing two doses of her anticoagulant. She was found to have an occlusive DVT in the left lower extremity requiring surgical thrombectomy. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed the absence of the inferior vena cava with collaterals draining into the azygos vein. She had negative thrombophilia testing. The initial and recurrent thrombotic events were attributed to stagnant and turbulent blood flow due to anomalous venous drainage from the lower extremities.

The patient was started on a heparin infusion for anticoagulation and was evaluated by vascular surgery, who took her for percutaneous transluminal venous thrombectomy of the left lower extremity, with operative findings of an acute-on-chronic DVT. A mechanical thrombectomy was performed through a 16 French lightning catheter, followed by balloon angioplasty with a 12 mm x 4 cm high-pressure balloon of a tight stenosis in the left common iliac vein with stenting using a 20 mm x 80 mm wallstent. Post-dilation was performed with a 14 mm x 4 cm high-pressure balloon, and further mechanical thrombectomy was performed, with venography showing patent vessels thereafter. She experienced rapid and dramatic improvement in her symptoms after mechanical thrombectomy and was transitioned from infusional heparin back to rivaroxaban for outpatient anticoagulation. She was discharged on postoperative day 2.

evidence.quote: Congenital absence of the IVC is a rare anatomic anomaly that is only seen in about 0.0005% and 1% of the population []. In young patients with otherwise unexplained deep vein thrombosis, it can be present in up to 5% of cases []. One can easily and rationally conceptualize that the absence of this large caliber vessel would cause turbulence and relatively static venous return to the heart, predisposing to thrombotic events as part of a virtual triad as mentioned above. Interestingly, our patient had never experienced DVT symptoms prior to her first event four years prior to this presentation. She had adapted to the absence of the IVC through the development of large collateral venous structures that drained into the azygous vein to reach the central circulation. Azygos continuation of the IVC in the setting of congenital agenesis of the IVC has previously been reported in other cases []. The employment of the present patient as a long-haul truck driver caused further venous stasis on top of that posed by her anatomic anomaly and interruption in anticoagulation, which led to the rapid development of recurrent DVT.

summary.text: A 53-year-old long-haul truck driver with prior left-leg DVT four years earlier and hypothyroidism developed acute painful swollen left leg after running out of rivaroxaban two days earlier. She reported no family clotting/bleeding/cancer history and denied alcohol, tobacco or illicit-drug use. Duplex showed extensive femoral-to-calf DVT; Chest CT showed no evidence of PE, thoracic aortic pathology or parenchymal lung pathology, and imaging showed enlarged azygos and absent IVC with retroperitoneal collateral drainage. Prior outside-record-confirmed comprehensive thrombophilia testing was negative; labs were normal except mild anemia, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL. She received heparin; percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy revealed acute-on-chronic DVT; iliac stenosis was ballooned/stented and patency restored. Symptoms improved rapidly, rivaroxaban resumed, and she was discharged on POD 2. Authors attributed recurrence to anomalous venous drainage/stasis with long-haul driving and interruption of anticoagulation as contributors, and recommended indefinite anticoagulation for persistent anatomic risk. No long-term implementation or follow-up was reported.
